questions.q: Why does this lesson argue that a structured checklist is a better format for an LDV review than an unstructured "does anything look slow" pass?
options: Because checklists are required by Salesforce's certification exams
Because unstructured reviews are not permitted by Salesforce's terms of service
Because checklists eliminate the need to analyze an org's data model at all
Because LDV risk is genuinely multi-dimensional, and an org can look healthy on one axis while heading for trouble on another, which a structured pass through each dimension is more likely to catch
questions.explain: LDV risk spans multiple independent dimensions (read-path, write-path, volume-management), and a structured checklist is more likely to catch a risk on an axis that happens to look fine on the surface than an informal, unstructured review.

questions.q: When checking selectivity math as part of the Chapter 1 review questions, what volume should the math be checked against?
options: Only the object's current record count
The object's projected future volume, not just its current volume
The org's total number of licensed users
The number of custom fields defined on the object
questions.explain: A filter that's comfortably selective today can drift toward or past the threshold as an object grows, so the review checklist explicitly calls for checking selectivity against projected volume, not just the current count.

questions.q: What is the recommended Chapter 2 checklist technique for flagging ownership or parent skew before it causes an incident?
options: Running SOQL aggregate checks that group records by OwnerId and by each major parent lookup field, flagging anything approaching the ~10,000-record guideline
Waiting for a bulk load to fail and diagnosing it after the fact
Disabling all lookup fields on the object
Requesting a skinny table for every object regardless of volume
questions.explain: Lesson 7's aggregate-query technique — grouping by owner or parent and sorting by count — is the proactive way to surface skew during a review, rather than waiting for a locking incident to reveal it.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what should happen after a checklist review produces a list of findings across all three chapters?
options: Every finding should be treated as equally urgent and fixed in the order discovered
Only the Chapter 1 findings matter; Chapter 2 and 3 findings can be ignored

Findings should be grouped by chapter, volume-management gaps that are making other findings worse should be identified, and recommendations should be sequenced so shrinking the active data set happens before or alongside more targeted fixes
The checklist itself is the final deliverable, with no further prioritization needed
questions.explain: A checklist produces findings, not a finished plan — the next step is grouping and sequencing them, informed by Lesson 14's triage framework and Lesson 15's case study, rather than treating every finding as independently and equally urgent.

questions.q: For data identified during a review as needing archiving (Chapter 3 checklist), what should already be evaluated before committing to a target?
options: Nothing further is needed once archiving is identified as necessary
Whether the data should instead be converted into a skinny table
Whether the org has enough Apex CPU time remaining for the current month
Whether the target (a Big Object or an external system) has constraints already evaluated against the specific data being moved into it
questions.explain: Per Lesson 12, a Big Object (or any archive target) comes with real constraints — field types, automation support, and so on — that need to be checked against the specific data being archived before committing to that target.
